source: Hoffmann & Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search
finding: FF estimates goal distance by solving the delete-relaxed task with a GRAPHPLAN-style planning graph and counting the actions in the extracted relaxed plan. It does not assume facts are independent, unlike HSP.
numbers: FF won the AIPS-2000 fully automatic track (Group A Distinguished Performance). Relaxed plans are found in polynomial time (proved); an optimal relaxed plan is NP-hard to find.
quote: estimates goal distances by ignoring delete lists
limits: Not provably efficient. Works empirically on benchmarks whose structure is simple; the authors say so.
agent_relevance: Relaxation means drop a constraint (here: nothing is ever undone), solve the easy task cheaply, and use its cost as the score for the real move.

source: Hoffmann & Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search
finding: HSP and FF use the same relaxation but combine it differently. HSP adds per-fact costs, which double counts shared steps. FF extracts one relaxed plan, which counts shared steps once.
numbers: Gripper example: with n balls left in room A, HSP rates picking up another ball 4n-2 and moving to room B 3n+1. With 4 or more balls left HSP prefers moving, which is wrong. FF prefers picking up.
limits: One hand-built example. Elsewhere FF's estimates are better than HSP's only by a small factor.
agent_relevance: When scoring a subgoal, count shared work once. Summing independent sub-scores overrates moves that look cheap alone.

source: Hoffmann & Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search
finding: Ablation over 20 domains of three switches: FF vs HSP distances, enforced hill-climbing vs plain hill-climbing, helpful actions on or off. FF distances beat HSP distances significantly in 8 to 10 domains per background setting and lost in only 5 cases overall. Enforced hill-climbing with helpful actions improved running time significantly in 16 of 20 domains and hurt in 1 (Fridge).
numbers: Without helpful actions, enforced hill-climbing got worse about as often as better. In Hanoi hill-climbing always restarts, because exponentially many steps give no better estimate.
limits: Significance is scattered across domains. Strong interaction between the techniques, specific to the domain.
agent_relevance: The relaxed score alone is a modest gain. Most of the speed came from using the relaxed result to prune choices (helpful actions) and from the search rule around it.

source: Hoffmann & Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search
finding: Helpful actions: use the relaxed plan to keep only applicable actions that add a fact the relaxed plan needs at its first step. The relaxation yields the candidate list for free.
numbers: Only 40% down to 5% of successors were helpful, falling as tasks grow. Schedule domain: 7,663 helpful successors out of 523,030 over 637 states in a size-50 task (about 2%).
limits: Incomplete: a constructed example loses all solutions. FF falls back to complete best-first search when it fails.
agent_relevance: Use the relaxed solution as a filter on which next steps to try, and fall back to the full set when the filtered search fails (G6: never stall).

source: Hoffmann & Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search
finding: Enforced hill-climbing: from the current state run breadth-first search until a state with a strictly better estimate appears, then commit. It works because better states are shallow.
numbers: Breadth-first almost always found a better state at depth 1, sometimes depth 2, very rarely depth 3, independent of task size. In Logistics with an optimal relaxed oracle the distance to a better state is at most d+1 (d = largest move distance), so the search is polynomial.
limits: Can get stuck in dead ends; then needs a restart with complete search.
agent_relevance: A short local look-ahead with the relaxed score is enough when the score is good. Go deeper only when the score fails to improve.

source: Hoffmann & Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search
finding: Where the relaxed estimate is poor, FF relies on other tricks. In Blocksworld the good results came mainly from goal ordering (goal agenda, added goal deletion), not from relaxed distance. The relaxation cannot see that stacking one block buries another.
numbers: FF solved about two thirds of the competition Blocksworld set. Plan lengths were 83% to 108% of System-R's (mean 96%); HSP2's were 97% to 177% (mean 153%). FF solved one size-50 task in 1.27 s; System-R needed 892.31 s.
limits: The unsolved instances are those where early goals block later ones.
agent_relevance: A relaxed subproblem cannot see the interaction it dropped. Add a separate check on subgoal order instead of a better relaxed estimate.

source: Hoffmann & Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search
finding: Choosing the best action order inside one relaxed layer is NP-complete, so FF accepts non-optimal relaxed plans. The heuristic is therefore not admissible and is used only for greedy search.
numbers: Theorem 2: deciding optimal action linearization is NP-complete. FF's experience was that greedy search works best when estimates are cautious (low).
limits: Footnote: even optimal linearization at each step would not make the whole relaxed plan optimal, so no admissibility.
agent_relevance: Two uses need two standards. To rank children, a cheap rough score is fine. To prove a bound, the score must never overestimate.

source: Hoffmann (2003) The Metric-FF Planning System: Translating Ignoring Delete Lists to Numeric State Variables
finding: Delete relaxation extends to numeric variables if the task is monotonic (higher values always better): ignore decreasing effects. Linear tasks can be rewritten into that form. Simply dropping constraints does not always simplify a task, so a dynamic relaxation is needed.
numbers: Metric-FF was one of the two most efficient numeric planners at IPC-3. In numeric Depots it solved most instances and was the only planner to solve the two largest; SemSyn solved only the smallest and MIPS 10.
limits: Only the monotonic or linear fragment. Not every relaxation is easy; you must check the relaxed task really is simpler.
agent_relevance: Before using a relaxed version, check that dropping the constraint really makes it easier, and that a real solution still counts as a relaxed solution.

source: Hoffmann (2005) Where 'Ignoring Delete Lists' Works: Local Search Topology in Planning Benchmarks
finding: Formal account of why delete relaxation works on benchmarks. Under idealised h+ (optimal relaxed plan length), 30 domains fall into a taxonomy of search landscapes.
numbers: 24 of 30 domains have no unrecognized dead ends. Of those 24, 17 have a constant bound on escape distance from local minima (13 have no local minima at all). Of those 17, 12 have a constant bound on escape from plateaus (bound 1 in 6 domains). In those 12, FF's search with h+ is a polynomial solver.
limits: h+ is NP-hard to compute. Results cover IPC benchmark encodings, which the author notes are simple.
agent_relevance: The relaxation helps where nothing is irreversible and subgoals do not interfere. Gate S0 could ask whether any step is irreversible; if so, relaxed scores will mislead.

source: Hoffmann (2005) Where 'Ignoring Delete Lists' Works: Local Search Topology in Planning Benchmarks
finding: Empirical check that FF's practical estimate hFF keeps the good landscape of h+. Method: sample 100 states per instance by random action sequences (length 0 to 2 times FF's plan length), compute exit distance by breadth-first search, and test whether each state lies on a valley (no path to goal along which hFF falls monotonically).
numbers: In the 11 other domains with no local minima under h+, 230 instance groups: one group had 5.0% of states on valleys, one 2.2%, eight below 1.0%, and 220 none. The exceptions were Grid and Hanoi (Hanoi 96% to 100% on valleys at larger sizes). Only one sample exceeded a proven bound (exit distance 2 instead of 1 in Logistics).
limits: Sampling by random walks, not exhaustive. 20 domains tested; of 10 IPC-3/4 domains only three have positive properties.
agent_relevance: Where the relaxation fails it fails hard (Hanoi, where undoing is essential). Expect domain-by-domain failure, so measure the relaxed score against real outcomes per problem class.

source: Hoffmann (2005) Where 'Ignoring Delete Lists' Works: Local Search Topology in Planning Benchmarks
finding: hFF and h+ have provably the same dead-end behaviour: a state with no relaxed plan has no real plan. The danger is the reverse, states with a relaxed plan but no real plan (unrecognized dead ends).
numbers: Rovers example: taking a soil sample with a rover that cannot reach the lander is an unrecognized dead end, because the sample exists only once and the relaxation never uses it up.
limits: Relaxation can only prove impossibility, never possibility.
agent_relevance: A relaxed check is a one-way test. Failing the relaxed version proves the real task unsolvable. Passing proves nothing.

source: Helmert (2006) The Fast Downward Planning System
finding: Fast Downward uses a different relaxation family, the causal graph heuristic, which decomposes the task by variable dependencies and ignores cycles. It adds preferred operators (helpful actions inside best-first search), deferred evaluation and multi-heuristic best-first search.
numbers: 550 STRIPS tasks from IPC1-3, 300 s limit. Unsolved tasks: FF 32, LPG 101, original causal-graph planner 25, the six Fast Downward configurations 21 to 32 (focused iterative broadening 148). Best-of-six solves all but 10 of 550. The best configuration solves everything except Depot and Freecell.
limits: Depot stays hard; the author blames lack of FF's goal-ordering help. IPC benchmarks only.
agent_relevance: Two different relaxations in one search beat one. Different cheap scores catch different mistakes. This fits G4 only if they differ in kind, not as samples of one model.

source: Helmert (2006) The Fast Downward Planning System
finding: In the multi-valued form, a variable's set of reachable values only grows in the relaxation, so applying an operator never makes a solvable relaxed task unsolvable. That monotonic progress is why the relaxed task is easy.
numbers: Blocksworld, 35 tasks, unsolved: FF 4, original causal-graph planner 0, most Fast Downward configurations 0 (focused broadening 17). Fast Downward's own FF heuristic does not always build the same relaxed plan as FF and was judged equally informative.
limits: Optimal relaxed plans remain NP-hard (Bylander 1994).
agent_relevance: The property to test for any easy version is monotonic progress: a step never ruins what earlier steps achieved.

source: Korf (1997) Finding Optimal Solutions to Rubik's Cube Using Pattern Databases
finding: Pattern databases are the abstraction route to a heuristic: solve a projection of the problem (only some cubies) exactly, store the exact cost, and use it as an admissible lower bound in IDA*. First optimal solutions to random Rubik's Cube instances.
numbers: State space 4.3252e19. Corner table 42 MB (expected value 8.764 moves), two 6-edge tables 20 MB each; total 82 MB, built in about 1 hour; the max of the three has expected value 8.878. Ten random instances: one needed 16 moves, three 17, six 18. About 700,000 nodes/s. Depth-16 search about 9.5 billion nodes (under 4 hours), depth 17 about 122 billion (about 2 days).
limits: One puzzle, one goal state; tables are built once per goal and the cost is amortized.
agent_relevance: Abstraction is a second kind of relaxation: ignore some details, solve the rest exactly, reuse the answer. For an LLM: solve a slice exactly in code, cache it, use it as a bound or filter.

source: Korf (1997) Finding Optimal Solutions to Rubik's Cube Using Pattern Databases
finding: Hypothesis: search time is about n/m (state space size over memory). Larger pattern databases give higher heuristic values and faster search. Taking the max of several tables is admissible.
numbers: Edge-cubie Manhattan distance expected 5.5 moves vs 8.764 for the corner table. Disk lookups (about 100 per second) would be about 7000 times slower than memory (700,000 nodes/s).
limits: Korf says this is an observation from data and intuition, not a formal analysis.
agent_relevance: A stronger relaxation pays off only until search cost stops falling; count the setup cost (G7).

source: Helmert & Domshlak (2009) Landmarks, Critical Paths and Abstractions: What's the Difference Anyway?
finding: Unifies four families of relaxation heuristics: delete relaxation (h+), critical paths (h^m), abstractions (pattern databases, merge-and-shrink) and landmarks. Proves dominance results and introduces the landmark-cut heuristic hLM-cut, an admissible approximation of h+.
numbers: Additive critical-path heuristics with m>=2 and merge-and-shrink abstractions strictly dominate landmark heuristics and additive hmax. Pattern databases are incomparable with both. hLM-cut gave the perfect h+ value on at least 72% of tasks; its average error was about 7 times lower than the next best (hLA, error 1.94) and its relative error 3.8 times lower.
limits: Theory is about admissible heuristics for optimal planning; dominance is about heuristic value, not runtime. hLA is more accurate on FreeCell and Openstacks.
agent_relevance: No single relaxation is best, so choose by problem class and combine. Landmarks are facts every solution must pass, usable as forced subgoals.

source: Helmert & Domshlak (2009) Landmarks, Critical Paths and Abstractions: What's the Difference Anyway?
finding: Optimal-planning test: A* with hLM-cut and LM-A* with hLA each solved more than 400 tasks over 22 domains; the next best planner, Gamer, solved 312.
numbers: The margin between the two best and Gamer is about twice the margin between Gamer and blind search. hLM-cut is a top performer in 16 of 22 domains; clear exceptions are Gripper and FreeCell.
limits: Table column totals were garbled in text extraction; figures here are from the paper's prose.
agent_relevance: Better relaxed estimates solve many more tasks at equal budget, but only where the estimate is accurate.

source: Correa, Pereira, Seipp et al. (2025) Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code
finding: Instead of a hand-made relaxation, the LLM writes a domain-specific heuristic as Python code. 25 candidates per domain are scored on training tasks in greedy best-first search; the best is run on larger unseen tasks (8 domains, 90 test tasks each, 720 total).
numbers: Total coverage out of 720, Pyperplan: DeepSeek R1 heuristic 373, DeepSeek V3 343, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking 305, hFF 234 (text; a table prints 243). R1 solved almost 40% more Blocksworld tasks than the second best. API cost for all V3 and R1 heuristics: $0.25 and $6.12.
limits: Needs a formal PDDL description. Choosing the heuristic by training score is itself heuristic. Pyperplan is slow next to C++ planners.
agent_relevance: The model proposes a scoring function, code tests it on held-out tasks, code selects. This fits G3 and G5 and has a measured gain over the classic relaxation heuristic under the same search.

source: Correa, Pereira, Seipp et al. (2025) Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code
finding: LLM heuristics in Python also compete with C++ Fast Downward relaxation heuristics and with a learned heuristic.
numbers: Total coverage out of 720: Fast Downward hFF 295, hadd 324, hcg 318, learned hGWPLRF 371; Pyperplan with R1 heuristic 373, V3 343. Floortile is the only domain where the best heuristic was not LLM-generated.
limits: Per-domain rows were interleaved in text extraction, so only totals are used. Fast Downward expands up to 669 times more states per second than Pyperplan.
agent_relevance: LLM-written heuristics can match strong hand-designed relaxations. The model replaces the design step, not the search.

source: Correa, Pereira, Seipp et al. (2025) Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code
finding: Writing the heuristic beats end-to-end planning by the same model by a wide margin, and a few samples are enough.
numbers: Solved tasks, end-to-end vs heuristic generation: Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking 202 to 305; DeepSeek R1 174 to 373. Distilled R1 Qwen 14B was the only generator below hFF. Going from 1 to 5 sampled heuristics gave the largest coverage jump, then diminishing returns; n=25 was used.
limits: Same benchmark family; test tasks are larger but of the same domains.
agent_relevance: Use the model as designer of the easy scorer, not as the planner. Sample about 5 to 25 candidates and select by held-out score.

source: Correa, Pereira, Seipp et al. (2025) Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code
finding: Prompt ablation: removing parts of the prompt hurt. Without example heuristics all generated heuristics scored coverage 0.
numbers: Best coverage with the original prompt 423, which is 38.7% above the next best ablation as the paper states it; worst coverage across ablations 63 to 138; average 237 to 270. Removing the Pyperplan code raised average coverage slightly but increased failing heuristics (of 200) by almost 50%.
limits: One model (Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking), 25 heuristics per setting.
agent_relevance: Worked examples of heuristics matter. Put exemplar scoring functions in the operator prompt.

source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi (2024, v3 2026) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through The Lens of Efficiency
finding: Argues that LLM-in-the-loop search methods (ToT, RAP, LATS, ReAct) are neither sound nor complete and spend many LLM calls. Proposes asking the LLM once to write the successor function and goal test as code, then running ordinary search.
numbers: 24 game: ToT reports 75% on 100 medium problems with about 100 LLM calls; the code approach solved all 1362 problems (100%) with on average 1.2 interactions for the successor function and 1 for the goal test. Mini crosswords: all 20 games solved by all five generated implementations, 5.5 s to 346 s total. Heuristic function left to future work.
limits: Four small search problems with small state spaces; needs a clear successor function.
agent_relevance: The cheapest simplification is moving rules into code once. Matches our rule: program decides, model fills a slot.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
finding: Step-back prompting: first ask the model for the high-level concept or principle behind the question, then reason from it. An LLM version of solving the abstract version first.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4% to 73.2% (+7), Chemistry 70.9% to 81.8% (+11); TimeQA 41.5% to 66% (+27 without retrieval is the abstract's figure), 68.7% with retrieval; MuSiQue +7. GPT-4 with chain-of-thought: physics 82.9% vs step-back 84.5%, chemistry 85.3% vs 85.6%. Llama2-70B physics 51.9% to 64.8%.
limits: With GPT-4 the gain over chain-of-thought is 1.6 and 0.3 points. Step-back fixed 20.5% of baseline errors and introduced 11.9% new ones (MMLU physics). Authors' own results.
agent_relevance: Abstraction first helps weaker models and fact-heavy tasks; the gain shrinks with a stronger model. Test per model.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
finding: Error analysis: the abstraction step rarely fails; the concrete reasoning that follows does.
numbers: On MMLU physics more than 90% of remaining errors are in the Reasoning step (Principle Error is small). On TimeQA more than half of errors are reasoning errors and 45% come from failing to retrieve the right information.
limits: Authors annotated their own wrong predictions on one set.
agent_relevance: The abstract step is easy for the model; executing the concrete steps is where it breaks. Put the checks after the concrete step.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Least-to-most prompting: split a hard problem into easier subproblems and solve them in order, feeding earlier answers into later ones. Aim is easy-to-hard generalization.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: 99.7% with 14 exemplars vs chain-of-thought 16.2% (standard prompting 16.7%). Last-letter concatenation, list length 12: 74.0% vs chain-of-thought 38.4% (8 exemplars; 37.4% with 4).
limits: GSM8K gain is small overall: 60.97% to 62.39%; on problems needing at least 5 steps 39.07% to 45.23%. Almost every failure could be solved with a hand-written decomposition, so the model's own decomposition is the weak point.
agent_relevance: Decomposing into easier versions gives large gains for generalizing to longer cases and small gains on ordinary math. The decomposition itself must be right.

source: Pearl (1984) Heuristics: Intelligent Search Strategies for Computer Problem Solving
finding: Pearl's thesis as cited by the FF and Helmert papers: heuristics are the exact costs of relaxed (simplified) versions of the problem, found by removing constraints; relaxed solutions give lower bounds and therefore admissible estimates.
numbers: Book not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Known only through citations in papers I read.
agent_relevance: Source of the idea behind operator O4 (drop a constraint).

source: Culberson & Schaeffer (1998) Pattern Databases
finding: Introduced pattern databases on the Fifteen Puzzle (Korf 1997 cites the 1996 version as the origin). The PDF fetch returned an HTML error page.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Download failed.
agent_relevance: Origin of abstraction heuristics; see Korf's account above.

source: Bonet & Geffner (2001) Planning as Heuristic Search
finding: HSP, the first successful domain-independent delete-relaxation planner, based on Bonet, Loerincs and Geffner (1997) per the FF paper. A search summary of Metric-FF says McDermott (1996) proposed the idea independently.
numbers: Not opened (download returned an HTML page).
limits: Known only through FF and Metric-FF text.
agent_relevance: Provenance of the delete-relaxation idea.

source: Hoffmann, Porteous & Sebastia (2004) Ordered Landmarks in Planning
finding: Landmarks are facts that must be true at some point in every plan, plus orderings between them, used as a chain of subgoals. The PDF text extraction was garbled, so I did not read it.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: PDF unreadable here.
agent_relevance: Landmarks as forced intermediate subgoals; Helmert & Domshlak (2009) relate them to relaxation.
